prose:notation-collisions:
A handful of common letters carry overloaded meanings in the literature. One enforces the following conventions throughout this paper to disambiguate them:

  • c = color (never charm; charm is \mathfrak{c}).

  • b = generic variable (never bottom quark; bottom is \mathfrak{b}).

  • p = brane point (never proton number; proton number is Z).

  • E alone = not used for an exceptional divisor, energy, or elliptic curve. One uses \mathcal{S}_p, \mathfrak{E}, or \mathcal{E}_q respectively. E_{\mathfrak{H}} (with hadron subscript) is allowed for crossing energy.

  • \mathfrak{E} bare = the energy \mathfrak{m}\,c_q^2 of a braid class (mass--energy equivalence). Every other energy carries a subscript: \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{cross}} (crossing energy, which is a different quantity), \mathfrak{E}_0, \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}}, \mathfrak{E}_{\gamma}, \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{pole}}. The Euler–Lagrange operator is \mathrm{EL}.

  • \mathfrak{E}_0 vs Q_\beta(n) — two distinct hadronic-sector scalars historically conflated in Python compute scripts. They are not interchangeable:

    • \mathfrak{E}_0 = hadronic energy scale. One derives this as \mathfrak{E}_0^{(N=0)} = m_e/(q_0(q_0-1)) \approx 4.186 MeV (from m_e and q_0 only). The tower-summed form is \mathfrak{E}_0^{\text{full}} = \mathfrak{E}_0^{(N=0)}/(1-\hbar_q^2) \approx 4.228 MeV. It sets the MeV-per-dimensionless-trace-unit conversion for hadronic predictions.
    • Q_\beta(n) = 0.78233341\,\text{MeV} = the free-neutron \beta-decay Q-value. One relates this to the bar-skew \beta-channel (P_{\mathrm{skew}}^{\beta}). One uses it as the binding-energy-scale multiplier in Categorical mass as Markov trace's explicit binding formula B = Q_\beta(n) \cdot (|\mathrm{tr}_M(W_{\text{free}})| - |\mathrm{tr}_M(W_{\text{atom}})|). The ratio is \mathfrak{E}_0/Q_\beta(n) = 1/|\Delta(\mathrm{net})| \approx 5.31 (the dimensionless Hecke NF reduction). Using \mathfrak{E}_0 for a Q_\beta-valued binding-scale quantity is a registered notation violation.

  • \gamma = three reserved meanings, all standard, disambiguated by context: (i) the photon (default reading in particle / QED contexts: pair production \gamma\gamma \to e^+ e^-, photonic channels, Breit–Wheeler vertices); (ii) the Euler–Mascheroni constant (only inside zeta-value identities, e.g. \zeta'(0) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi), \gamma = \lim(H_n - \log n)); (iii) Dirac matrices \gamma^\mu (always with an explicit Lorentz index). One never uses \gamma for a vortex or closed cycle — the vortex morphism is \varrho.

  • c_k vs \mathrm{cl}_k — the letter c carried three distinct coefficient families, two of them within ~12% of each other numerically, which is how they stayed conflated. One now splits them:

    • c_k = Q_\beta precision-ladder coefficients only, Q_\beta = Q_{\text{base}}\prod_k(1 + c_k u^k) with u = b\hbar_q^2 — dimensionless, c_2 = -1, c_3 = -2 a near-match. (This register fixes the symbol; each rung's epistemic tier and its convention scoping live in the c_k/d_k canonical registry. The word "proved" previously appeared on c_2 here and is removed as a symbol-level claim — the identity re-reads the N{=}2 factor rather than deriving it. "Taylor-exact" was NOT removed for being false, and must not be: c_2 genuinely is the u^2 coefficient of the explicit-factor product \prod_{k\ge2}(1 + c_k u^k). It is \tilde c_2 = -9/8 only for the normalised series with the cosine factor inside — so always say which series. No tier is changed by this edit.)
    • \tilde c_k = the normalised-series coefficients of the same ladder model: the u^k coefficients of \Phi(u)/\Phi(0) rather than of the explicit factors. The tilde marks a different normalisation of the same object — deliberately not justified by the old w_\lambda / \tilde w_\lambda pairing, which this same register retired in the entry below. The two families are not interchangeable: the model's cosine factor contributes at every order, and \tilde c_2 = c_2 - 1/8 exactly, independently of the phase \alpha, so the committed c_2 = -1 has \tilde c_2 = -9/8. Both are correct — one model at two normalisations. The -1/8 is contributed entirely by the half-argument in \cos(\alpha - u/2).
    • c_k^{\mathrm{even}} = the bar-even part of the ladder data, exact in \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt 3) — a third object, read as neither c_k nor \tilde c_k.
    • \mathrm{cl}_k = cluster / Ursell coefficients of the many-body expansion — MeV-valued. \mathrm{cl}_3 = -\mathfrak{E}_0\,\Delta^2 g is the three-body cluster coefficient of the \mu_3 door (\mu_3 > 0 \iff \Delta^2 g < 0), and the Borromean H_9 magnitude lift is the same family. One never writes a bare c_k for a cluster coefficient, and never quotes a c_k value without saying which of c_k / \tilde c_k / c_k^{\mathrm{even}} it is — the three differ at the same k (-1, -9/8, \approx -7.4588 at k = 2). Rationale for the roman two-letter tag rather than a new single letter: every single Roman letter is either register-claimed or produces a same-domain case-collision (X_k vs the knot object X_K; Y_k vs the Markov weight y_\lambda; Z = proton number; W_\lambda = geometric weight; j vs the Jones polynomial J_K(q)). This follows the same resolution already used for \mathrm{Sk} (Skein module, moved off \mathcal{S}) and h_{\mathrm{A}} (Hecke amplitude, moved off bare H_A).

  • \chi_q = Lyapunov exponent (distinct from \chi_\zeta(c), the character).

  • Euler characteristic is \chi_{\mathrm{eu}} — never a bare \chi. The glyph \chi is shared by three register-claimed families: the characters \chi_\lambda (Frobenius pairing \mathrm{tr}_M = \sum_\lambda y_\lambda \chi_\lambda) and \chi_\zeta(c); the Lyapunov exponent \chi_q above; and the Euler characteristic, which keeps the standard glyph but always carries the roman subscript: \chi_{\mathrm{eu}}. A bare \chi is a notation violation in all three senses. Remark Hom-set. Hom-set. For objects X and Y in a category \mathbf{C}, the hom-set \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y) is the collection of all morphisms from X to Y. It is also written \mathbf{C}(X, Y) or X \to Y. In a locally small category, each hom-set is a genuine set.

When \mathbf{C} is R-linear, each hom-set carries the structure of an R-module. Composition is R-bilinear.
rem:glossary-monoidal-category: Remark Monoidal category. Monoidal category. A category \mathbf{C} equipped with a bifunctor \otimes \colon \mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}, a distinguished unit object \mathbf{1}, and coherent natural isomorphisms for associativity (\alpha), left unitality (\lambda), and right unitality (\rho). These satisfy Mac Lane's pentagon and triangle axioms.
rem:glossary-braided-monoidal-category: Remark Braided monoidal category. Braided monoidal category. A monoidal category equipped with a natural isomorphism \beta_{X,Y} \colon X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \otimes X satisfying the two hexagon axioms.
rem:glossary-symmetric-monoidal-category: Remark Symmetric monoidal category. Symmetric monoidal category. A braided monoidal category whose braiding is involutive: \beta_{Y,X} \circ \beta_{X,Y} = \mathrm{id}_{X \otimes Y}.
rem:glossary-monoidal-functor:
Remark Monoidal functor. Monoidal functor. A functor F \colon \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D} between monoidal categories equipped with a natural transformation \mu_{X,Y} \colon F(X) \otimes F(Y) \to F(X \otimes Y) and a morphism \epsilon \colon \mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{D}} \to F(\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{C}}). These are compatible with the associator and unitors.

The functor is lax monoidal when \mu and \epsilon are arbitrary morphisms and strong monoidal when they are isomorphisms.
sec:glossary-rigidity-intro: This section defines the rigidity, duality, and pivotal-category terminology used throughout this paper.
rem:glossary-exact-pairing:
Remark Exact pairing. Exact pairing. Given objects X and Y in a monoidal category, an exact pairing consists of morphisms \varepsilon \colon X \otimes Y \to \mathbf{1} (evaluation) and \eta \colon \mathbf{1} \to Y \otimes X (coevaluation) satisfying the snake identities:

(\varepsilon \otimes \mathrm{id}_X) \circ (\mathrm{id}_X \otimes \eta) = \mathrm{id}_X, \qquad (\mathrm{id}_Y \otimes \varepsilon) \circ (\eta \otimes \mathrm{id}_Y) = \mathrm{id}_Y.

When an exact pairing exists, Y is a right dual of X, and X a left dual of Y.
rem:glossary-left-dual: Remark Left dual. Left dual. An object Y in a monoidal category has a left dual if there exists an object X and an exact pairing (X, Y).
rem:glossary-right-dual: Remark Right dual. Right dual. An object X in a monoidal category has a right dual if there exists an object Y and an exact pairing (X, Y).
rem:glossary-rigid-category: Remark Rigid category. Rigid category. A monoidal category in which every object has both a left dual and a right dual.
rem:glossary-pivotal-category:
Remark Pivotal category. Pivotal category. A rigid monoidal category equipped with a monoidal natural isomorphism \delta_X \colon X \xrightarrow{\sim} X^{\vee\vee} between each object and its double dual.

The pivotal structure is what makes a left trace definable alongside the right one: without \delta there is no way to close the left-hand loop back onto X, since evaluation lands on X^{\vee\vee}. A pivotal category in which the two traces then agree on every object is called spherical; pivotal alone does not force that agreement. The left quantum dimension, defined through the inverse braiding, is in general a different morphism from the right one, so sphericality is an additional hypothesis rather than a consequence of the pivotal structure.

The name is geometric [barrett1993]. Regard S^2 as the plane with a point at infinity adjoined: carrying a loop closed on the right to the same loop closed on the left drags it past that point, a move available on S^2 but not in \mathbb{R}^2. A pivotal category evaluates closed diagrams invariantly under isotopy of the plane, and a spherical one under isotopy of the sphere. The picture interprets the condition \mathrm{tr}_L = \mathrm{tr}_R rather than deriving it, and the condition can fail: in the quantised enveloping algebra of the Borel subalgebra of \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C}) the two traces are \mathrm{tr}(\theta w) and \mathrm{tr}(\theta w^{-1}) for the pivotal element w, and they differ [barrett1993].
rem:glossary-compact-closed-category: Remark Compact closed category. Compact closed category. A symmetric monoidal category that is also rigid. Since the braiding identifies X \otimes Y \cong Y \otimes X, left duals and right duals coincide.
rem:glossary-r-linear-category: Remark R-linear category. R-linear category. A category whose hom-sets carry the structure of R-modules (for a commutative ring R) such that composition is R-bilinear.
rem:glossary-no-quasi-zeros:
Remark Algebra without quasi-zeros. Let R be a commutative ring with unity and A an R-algebra. An element a \in A is a quasi-zero if

  bac = 0 \qquad \text{for all } b, c \in A \text{ not both } 1.

The algebra A is without quasi-zeros if no such element exists. Assume that R has no quasi-zeros. This ensures that leading-term decompositions are well-defined and the division algorithm terminates correctly. It guarantees that R-linear hom-spaces have no phantom morphisms annihilated by all compositions, making the Frobenius pairing non-degenerate.
rem:glossary-cemetery-group: Remark Cemetery group. Cemetery group. The cemetery group \mathcal{Z}_n \subset \mathcal{K}_n is the localising subcategory of graded projective KLR modules annihilated by the fibre functor \tau. It acts as a homological pruning filter on the Gröbner–Shirshov reduction engine. A state word that lands in \mathcal{Z}_n is buried: its image under any subsequent observation vanishes, allowing the computation branch to be dropped.

rem:glossary-quantum-flatness:
Remark Quantum flatness. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with gauge group G_q = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) and connection \nabla on A. Let \mathrm{INN}(G_q) denote the inner-automorphism 2-group of G_q, with 2-form datum B \in \Omega^2(A) \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(A).

The connection \nabla is quantum flat if the curvature F_\nabla equals the 2-form datum:

  F_\nabla = B.

This is not an independent axiom. It is a derived consequence of the instanton condition combined with the simplicity constraint B \in \Gamma(\Lambda^+ H^* \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(P)):

\begin{equation}\label{eq:quantum-flatness-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  F_\nabla \ar[r, equal, "\text{instanton}"]
    \ar[dr, equal, "F_\nabla = B"']
  & F_\nabla^+ \ar[d, equal, "\text{simplicity}"] \\
  & B
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\text{(quantum flatness)}
\end{equation}

The instanton equation \star_q F_\nabla = F_\nabla forces self-dual curvature. The simplicity constraint restricts B = F_\nabla^+. Therefore F_\nabla = B. Quantum flatness encodes the condition that the 2-group gauge theory of \mathrm{INN}(G_q) admits no independent 2-connection. The ordinary connection fully determines the 2-form datum.
rem:glossary-reeb-gauge-group:
Remark The Reeb gauge group U_1(R). Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe over R with maximal torus T and Reeb derivation \xi. The Reeb gauge group is the R-group scheme

  U_1(R)  :=  T
  =  \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau|_{\langle V \rangle})

which is the maximal torus of the gauge group G. Over \mathbb{C}, this recovers U(1). Over a general commutative ring R, it is the multiplicative group of norm-one elements in the rank-one weight lattice.

The Reeb gauge group plays six simultaneous roles, all arising from T \subset G:

  1. Gauge group of the Reeb fibre. The projective line \mathbb{P}(V) = G/T is a principal U_1(R)-bundle. The fibre over each point is a copy of T acting by scalar multiplication on the weight spaces. The Reeb derivation \xi is the infinitesimal generator of this U_1(R)-action.
  2. Weight grading. The U_1(R)-action on \Omega^k(A) induces the weight decomposition \alpha = \alpha_H + \alpha_V: \alpha_H \in \ker(\iota_\xi) (weight 0) and \alpha_V (non-zero weight). The characters of U_1(R) label the weights.
  3. Contact structure. The contact affine chart U_\xi \subset \mathbb{P}(V) is the complement of the U_1(R)-fixed locus. The contact form \varTheta_A satisfies \varTheta_A(\xi) = 1 and \iota_\xi d\varTheta_A = 0, defining a connection on the U_1(R)-bundle.
  4. Commutative observation direction. In the adjoint bundle \mathrm{Ad}(J^1\mathcal{S}), the U_1(R)-direction is the Cartan subalgebra. It is the one direction in the colour fibre where intents commute: [\mathfrak{O}_1, \mathfrak{O}_2] = 0 when both act along \xi. Fermionic uncertainty lives in the remaining two directions.
  5. Longitudinal backbone. In the harmonic decomposition of H^1(\mathcal{S}_n, \mathrm{ad}\mathcal{S}_n), the U_1(R)-modes are the longitudinal backbone: steady-state flows aligned with the Reeb direction.
  6. Arrow of time. The Reeb flow \phi_t^q is the one-parameter subgroup generated by \xi. Under the braiding-induced ordering \prec_c, forward time is the direction of this flow.
rem:glossary-categorical-transport:
Remark Categorical transport equation. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe with instanton \nabla and q-deformed exterior derivative d_q. The categorical transport equation for a section \psi \in \tau(J^1(A)) is

\begin{equation}\label{eq:categorical-transport}
  \hbar_q\pi_V(\nabla\psi) =  \hat{H}_q(\psi),
\end{equation}

where \hat{H}_q \colon \tau(J^1(A)) \to \tau(J^1(A)) is the q-Hamiltonian endomorphism \hat{H}_q = -\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar_q\Delta_q + V_q, with V_q the potential arising from the curvature F_\nabla. The following diagram encodes the transport:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:transport-cd}
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em]
  \tau(J^1(A)) \ar[r, "\nabla"] \ar[d, "j^1"']
  & \tau(J^1(A)) \otimes \Omega^1 \ar[d, "\pi_V"] \\
  \tau(A) \ar[r, "\hat{H}_q"']
  & \tau(J^1(A))
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
rem:glossary-categorical-q-torsion-leaf:
Remark Categorical q-torsion leaf. A q-torsion leaf is a maximal sub-object L \hookrightarrow A such that:

  1. Horizontality: L \subset \ker(\pi_V) (all forms on L are horizontal).
  2. Flow invariance: \phi_t^q(L) = L for all t (the q-Reeb flow preserves L).
rem:glossary-aether:
Remark Aether. Aether. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe. Its aether is the self-dual Frobenius–Hopf algebra object A of \mathbf{C} (Frobenius–Hopf substrate). The aether parameter is the scalar q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) of substrate parameter; it is a coordinate on the fibre \mathbb{G}_m, not on the base (base, not fibre). A quantity is aether-derived when it is built from q and the categorical data (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) alone.

The aether is a categorical object with no state of motion, in the sense of Einstein's ether. Three neighbouring notions are distinct from it:

  • the brane is a base object, not the aether (brane);
  • the algebraic layer is the class of statements valid over a generic commutative ring R, before the algebraic→archimedean wall; it is a layer of statements, not an object;
  • a base ring (the adeles \mathbb{A}, a motivic or Hahn coefficient ring) is a ring of coefficients, not the aether.
rem:glossary-brane:
Remark Brane. Brane. In the recursive brane tower A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow \cdots, the object A_n is the brane of A_{n+1}: the base object of which A_{n+1} = T(A_n) is the tangent algebra. The derived usages keep this base sense: the brane boundary \partial A_n is a full subcategory of subobjects of A_n; a brane point is a point p of the base manifold M, blown up to the exceptional divisor carrying the Reeb bundle; the brane fluid is the fluid on the base.

A brane is a base, while the aether parameter q rides on the fibre. The brane is therefore not the aether.
rem:glossary-descent: Remark Descent. Let (\mathbf{C}, A, \tau) be a quantum observable universe and let \{A_n\}_{n \geq 0} be the recursive brane tower. The descent is the reverse traversal of the tower. Passage from level n to level n{-}1 applies the restriction morphism r_n \colon A_n = J^1(A_{n-1}) \to A_{n-1}. In the archimedean realisation, this restricts the connection and bundle to the base manifold M_{n-1}. The descent terminates in finitely many steps, bounded by \mathrm{Krulldim} Z(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A)).
rem:glossary-s3-group:
Remark Symmetric group S_3. Imposing the involution relations \sigma_i^2=\mathrm{id} on the braid group B_3 yields the symmetric group S_3:

\begin{equation}\label{eq:s3-presentation}
  S_3
  =\bigl\langle s_1,s_2
     \big| s_1^2=s_2^2=(s_1 s_2)^3=\mathrm{id}\bigr\rangle.
\end{equation}
rem:glossary-q-bit:
Remark The q-bit: unit of q-deformed information. A q-bit is the natural unit of information in a QOU with aether parameter q. It is the information generated by one application of the q-connection \nabla_q across a fibre, which corresponds to one crossing resolution in the Iwahori--Hecke algebra H_n(q) or one iteration of the quadratic map f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q) on the exceptional divisor.

Definition. One q-bit = \eta_q in classical natural units, where

  \eta_q =  \frac{2q - 1}{q^3}

is the operational entropy.

The two Hecke eigenvalues. The name "q-bit" reflects the Iwahori--Hecke algebra's two eigenvalues q (symmetric channel) and -q^{-1} (antisymmetric channel). At q = 1 the eigenvalues merge to \pm 1 and one q-bit equals one classical nat.

Values.

q \eta_q (q-bits = classical nats) Regime
1 1.000 Classical limit (one q-bit = one nat)
q_0 0.892 The observed universe
\varphi^2 0.327 Golden threshold
\infty 0 Big Bang (no information)

"It from q-bit." Wheeler's "it from bit" asserts that physics emerges from information. The QOU refines this: observable physics emerges from q-deformed information. The observability axiom forces every observable quantity to be a rational function of q. Each elementary process produces exactly one q-bit. The aether parameter q controls non-commutativity.
rem:glossary-q-bit-skein:
Remark One q-bit = one Skein operation. The q-bit–Skein identification of one q-bit with one Skein operation unifies several structures in this paper.

One q-bit = one crossing resolution

Each application of the Skein relation

  L_+ - L_- = (q - q^{-1})L_0

resolves one crossing. The resolution produces exactly one q-bit (= \eta_q) of information: the choice between the symmetric channel and the antisymmetric channel. The q-bit is the information content of this binary choice, weighted by the Hecke eigenvalues.

Transfer matrix as q-bit register

The categorical transfer matrix factorizes the Markov trace over generators:

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\rho(\beta))
  = 
  \prod_{i=0}^{n-2} \hat{V}_i(q).

Each vertex volume \hat{V}_i is a one-point correlation function. The transfer matrix is a register of q-bits: each generator \sigma_i stores one q-bit, and the Markov trace reads out the entire register. The transfer matrix product is the exact factorization of the n-point function into n-1 single-q-bit evaluations.

Physical processes as q-bit computations

Every physical process in the QOU is a q-bit computation:

Process q-bits consumed Mechanism
One Reeb iteration 1 q-bit One f_q evaluation on exceptional divisor
One Collatz cycle (v = 2) 3 q-bits 1 odd step + 2 even steps
Beta decay (T_{3,5}) 10 q-bits 10-crossing Skein resolution
One Planck time n_R = q/(q-1) q-bits Full Reeb circuit
Jones polynomial of c-crossing link c q-bits Full resolution tree

Beta decay consumes 10 q-bits because the weak boson T_{3,5} = (\sigma_1 \sigma_2)^5 has 10 crossings. Each crossing resolution is one q-bit.

Justification of Q_{\mathrm{cat}}

The categorical Q-value of a nuclear reaction is the net q-bit balance. It is the difference between the q-bits stored in the parent braid and the q-bits stored in the daughter braids. Because each crossing is one q-bit, the Q-value is the crossing number difference:

  Q_{\mathrm{cat}}
  = 
  \bigl(c_{\mathrm{parent}} - c_{\mathrm{daughter}}\bigr)
   \cdot  \eta_q
  \quad q\text{-bits}.

The crossing number is the exact q-bit content of the braid, and the Skein relation conserves q-bits at each resolution step.
rem:glossary-distinguished-triangle: Remark Distinguished triangle. Distinguished triangle. In an additive category \mathbf{T} with a shift functor X \mapsto X[1], a triangle is a diagram X \to Y \to Z \to X[1]. A pretriangulated structure on \mathbf{T} singles out a class of distinguished triangles, closed under isomorphism and rotation, containing X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}} X \to 0 \to X[1], such that every morphism X \to Y extends to a distinguished triangle, and satisfying the octahedral axiom; the distinguished triangles play the role that short exact sequences play in an abelian category, and a functor to an abelian category is homological when it sends them to long exact sequences.
rem:glossary-derived-category: Remark Derived category. Derived category. For an abelian category \mathbf{A}, the derived category D(\mathbf{A}) is the localisation of the category of cochain complexes in \mathbf{A} at the quasi-isomorphisms (the maps inducing isomorphisms on cohomology); equivalently, the localisation of the homotopy category of complexes at the same class. It is a triangulated category whose distinguished triangles come from short exact sequences of complexes. The bounded derived category D^{b}(\mathbf{A}) is the full subcategory of complexes with bounded cohomology, and D^{b}(X) for a variety X means D^{b} of coherent sheaves on X.
rem:glossary-dg-category: Remark Differential graded category. Differential graded category. A category enriched in cochain complexes over a commutative ring R: each hom-object \mathrm{Hom}(X, Y) is a complex of R-modules, composition is a chain map \mathrm{Hom}(Y, Z) \otimes \mathrm{Hom}(X, Y) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, Z), and identities are cycles of degree zero. Taking zeroth cohomology of every hom-complex gives an ordinary category, the homotopy category of the dg category; a dg category with one object is a dg algebra. Dg categories are the setting in which Hochschild homology of a category, and functoriality of Hochschild homology under derived functors, are defined without choices.
